sum: Recent commentary around Diageo (LSE:DGE) has zeroed in on Guinness, where management flagged a dip in UK and Ireland sales as younger drinkers tilt toward fruit-flavoured beers and premium lagers.

Against that backdrop, Diageo's recent momentum has picked up, with a 30-day share price return of 10.46% and a year to date share price gain of 19.53%, even though the 5-year total shareholder return has declined 43.06% as investors reassess both Guinness headwinds as well as the latest boardroom and trading updates.

Diageo shares have bounced hard while Guinness faces real pressure from changing tastes. Does that recent rally still offer a sensible balance of risk and reward once the valuation is stripped back?

On the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St, Diageo's fair value sits at £20.62 against a last close of £19.22, which frames the recent rebound as a move toward that estimate rather than away from it.

The main thing that has to go right is that Diageo executes the multi year restructuring and North America turnaround without major disruption, so the targeted overhead reductions, route to market changes and category strategies in key regions translate into sustained operating profit and free cash flow delivery.

The current valuation implies the share price already reflects cautious assumptions on near term net sales growth and North America pressure, so if Diageo delivers on its plan for mid single digit operating profit growth, material recurring savings and multi year capex behind Guinness, the stock appears undervalued on this narrative.

sum: Diageo (LSE: DGE) shares have staged a remarkable comeback, soaring 38% from their March lows. After a bruising period for the drinks giant, could this be the moment everything finally starts to turn around? Or are investors getting ahead of themselves?

Diageo's latest trading update looks like a bit of a mixed bag to me. There are reasons to be encouraged, with sales returning to growth and some of its biggest brands showing signs of strength. Guinness, whisky and Smirnoff Ice all delivered growth, while Latin America and Asia Pacific put in particularly good performances.

As an existing shareholder, that's encouraging. But I wouldn't conclude that the drinks giant is out of the woods. Far from it. Strip out the contribution from East African Breweries (EABL), which it's in the process of selling, and organic sales growth was a pretty modest 0.6%.

Management has kept its full-year forecasts unchanged too. That's hardly a ringing endorsement of a rapid recovery. For me, this is a small step in the right direction. So what could be the spark that ignites the next leg in the recovery?
For me, the biggest piece of the recovery puzzle is the US. After all, North America accounts for over a third of Diageo's total sales.

Unfortunately, the latest numbers don't make particularly encouraging reading. Organic sales in the region fell 3.6%, with volumes down 3.7%. That's concerning. Diageo isn't simply facing a problem with consumers trading down to cheaper alternatives. Its overall sales volumes are falling, while price and mix are contributing virtually nothing to growth.
This raises a bigger question for me. Is the cost-of-living squeeze changing the way Americans think about spending on alcohol?

sum: For the last five years, Diageo (LSE: DGE) shares have repeatedly fallen. There have been one or two jumps along the way, but they were never sustained. Until now…

Shares in the beleaguered FTSE 100 spirits maker have climbed almost 15% in the last month, lifting to around 1,877p. But they're still roughly 50% below their level five years' ago, when they traded either side of 4,000p. I'm not expecting them to recover their former glories any time soon, but is this a buying opportunity?
For years, Diageo was seen as one of the best blue-chip investments money could buy. Its global brands include Johnnie Walker, Captain Morgan, Tanqueray, Baileys and, of course, Guinness.

But investors lost faith amid falling sales and fears that people will continue to drink less because of health concerns and changing attitudes among younger generations. Weight-loss drugs may also be having an impact, along with the cost-of-living crisis. That's a nasty cocktail to contend with.

I think we can dismiss some of the gloomier predictions. Humans and our primate ancestors have been consuming alcohol for 10m years, and brewing it for at least 13,000. It would be rather odd if we all stopped around the time I added Diageo to my Self-Invested Personal Pension (SIPP), but you never know.
Turnaround specialist Sir Dave Lewis (aka Drastic Dave) arrived in January and promptly did the last thing investors wanted, slashing the dividend by more than 50%. The yield's now below 2%.

More positively, Lewis also launched a restructuring programme targeting $1bn of annual savings, simplified the business and agreed to sell its East African Breweries stake. He's also keen to take full advantage of the desire for Guinness and canned cocktails.

Adding these together, we can see that Alphabet shares have been particularly popular recently. Why might that be?

The reason is that the tech giant slumped more than 12% at the end of October, shedding more than $500bn in market value in one day. Indeed, after peaking at $399 in May, the stock has tumbled to $285. That’s a fall of almost 30%!

The first thing I need to remember is that volatility and periods of poor performance are par for the course for a long-term investor.
My holding period for a stock is three-to-five years (ideally longer). Therefore, what happens over three-to-five months isn't that important in the grand scheme of things.
That said, I'd be lying if I said I wasn't bothered when my portfolio rapidly declines in value. I don't like it. But I know it's the price of admission to the stock market.

As always, there's a Warren Buffett quote that clarifies things: "You've got to be prepared, when you buy a stock, to have it go down 50% — or more — and be comfortable with it, as long as you're comfortable with the holding."
Another thing I like to do at times like this is to put things into perspective. Returning to HSBC and BAE, for example, these UK shares had a fantastic 2025. So did Rolls-Royce.

Is the much-predicted stock market crash finally here?
sum: For several years, lots of investors and pundits have been predicting a stock market crash. AI valuations, among others, have looked dizzying. There has been a disconnection between the exuberance of the stock market and the outlook for much of the real-life economy.
This week has been a frantic and action-packed one in the stock market, especially Stateside and with massive negative impact on tech stocks.
Formally the answer is… not yet. A crash involves a fall of 20% or more in a short order of time. We have not reached that point.

However, that does not mean that the crash may not have already started. It could be that, if things continue as they have done in recent days, the cumulative losses hit 20%. We may look back in retrospect and say that this week marked the start of the crash.
Or we may not. Falling markets often bring out bargain hunters who want to scoop up shares at lower prices than before. That can help stabilise prices and restore confidence.
Still, the truth is that many market valuations look unsustainable to me.
Like everybody else though, I cannot know for sure when the stock market crash will next crash.

sum: Diageo reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 net sales of $4.931 billion for the period ended September 30, 2026, up 1.2% from the prior-year quarter. The company said trading was in line with expectations in its Fiscal 27 Q1 Trading Statement published on Thursday, November 5.

Organic net sales increased 1.4% including East African Breweries Limited and 0.6% excluding EABL. Organic volume excluding EABL slipped 0.1%, while price and mix added 0.7 percentage points. Whisky, Guinness and Smirnoff ready-to-drink products were among the reported growth drivers.

North American organic net sales declined 3.6%, reflecting continued market softness. Diageo said it is working to make its offer more competitive, but the region remains the group's biggest challenge.

Growth was stronger elsewhere. Asia Pacific organic net sales rose 4.1%, Latin America and the Caribbean increased 4.8%, India grew 3.4% and Europe, the Middle East and Africa advanced 2.4%. The regional mix gives investors a clearer view of where the group's recovery is gaining traction and where execution risks remain.

Diageo maintained its fiscal 2027 outlook for broadly flat organic net sales and low- to mid-single-digit organic operating profit growth. The company expects free cash flow of about $2 billion after exceptional costs linked to operating framework and supply-chain changes and excluding cash from EABL.

Diageo Holds Guidance, Shares Climb
sum: Diageo (LON: DGE), the maker of Johnnie Walker, Guinness and Smirnoff, left its full-year guidance unchanged in a first-quarter update this morning, and its shares rose after the statement. The release, headlined “In line with our expectations”, covers the quarter to the 30th of September.

The shares opened at 1,860p and were at 1,897p by 8:14am on a delayed quote, up 83p or 4.58% on yesterday’s close of 1,814p. The day’s range so far is 1,856p to 1,908p. That is above the previous 2026 closing high of 1,874p, set on the 24th of February.

Net sales were $4,931m, against $4,875m a year earlier, up 1.2% as reported and 1.4% organically (stripping out currency, acquisitions and disposals). Excluding EABL, the business being sold to Asahi, organic growth was 0.6%. Latin America, Asia Pacific, EMEA and India all grew. North America did not.
Chief executive Sir Dave Lewis addressed the weak region directly.
In North America, we continue to focus on making our offer more competitive, and whilst this remains our biggest challenge, clear actions are underway.

North America, 36% of net sales, fell 3.6% organically on a 3.7% volume drop. Don Julio, Casamigos and Crown Royal each declined by double digits, and a packaging quality issue hurt Casamigos ready-to-drink products.

Guidance for the 2027 financial year is unchanged from the capital markets day: broadly flat organic net sales, North America down by a mid-single-digit percentage, and organic operating profit up low-to-mid single digit. Free cash flow is put at about $2bn, against $3.2bn in the 2026 financial year, after about $850m of exceptional costs.

sum: As a shareholder in Diageo (LSE: DGE), am I likely to raise a glass to the distiller's performance any time soon? So far this year, the company has announced a big dividend cut – and Diageo shares have gained only slightly more than the FTSE 100 index of which the company is a member. The share price is up 10%, compared to 8% for the index.

Looking ahead though, some investors reckon a significant strategic realignment at the company could see Diageo shares soar. Some 54% cheaper than five years ago, they currently look more attractively priced than they did for years – if we believe the turnaround narrative.
However, my plan is to hold on to my shares for now without buying even one more.
That is because I reckon that from a medium- to long-term perspective, the turnaround strategy might not be the firecracker for the Diageo share price that some investors are hoping it is.

Sharply reducing the dividend saves money. Cutting jobs through layoffs and plant consolidation to streamline the supply chain can also do the same, even though in the short term it can actually add one-off costs.

Cost cuts could potentially help boost Diageo's financial performance and therefore its shares. In the medium term, it is targeting "attractive" growth in earnings per share ahead of organic operating profit growth (ignoring exchange rate movements).
But while investors may like the sound of cost-cutting financially, it can bring other problems.

sum: Diageo's (LSE:DGE) share price has endured quite a bumpy ride since Sir Dave Lewis took charge. The beverages giant saw its share price drop sharply after Lewis cut shareholder dividends back in February, kicking off his larger turnaround strategy.

Since then, the shares have remained volatile, albeit on a seemingly gradual upward trajectory. But beneath all this market motion, there seems to be a growing list of reasons to be optimistic about what's on the horizon for this enterprise. And it's why the analyst team at Bernstein have just issued a £24.40 share price target.
That's a roughly 39% projected rally over the next 12 months compared to where the stock's trading today – enough to take it back to levels last seen in late 2024.
So what needs to happen for this bullish forecast to become reality?

Cutting dividends rarely wins a new chief executive many friends, particularly among income investors who often head for the exits once the pool of potential passive income starts to dry up. However, in this instance, this painful move seems quite prudent.

It's no secret that Diageo's business has been struggling since the untimely passing of former CEO Sir Ivan Menezes back in 2023. And by reducing the amount of cash flow distributed to shareholders, Lewis gains a lot more flexibility to reduce leverage, strengthen the balance sheet, and reinvest in flagship brands.
That's seemingly what's gotten the team at Bernstein excited. While North America and China remain tricky markets, Diageo's seeing stronger results across most of the rest of the world.

British American Tobacco: The Biggest Paycheck in the Vice Bundle

British American Tobacco (NYSE:BTI | BTI Price Prediction) trades in the US as an American Depositary Receipt (ADR). An ADR is a dollar-denominated certificate on a US exchange that represents shares of a foreign company. You buy and sell it like any stock. But dividends are declared in British pounds and converted to dollars, so your dollar check moves with exchange rates. In 2022, for example, the quarterly ADR payment slipped to $0.66919 from $0.740411, even though the company did not cut its pound dividend.

Dividend safety: Trailing 12-month ADR dividends of $3.253621 against trailing EPS of $3.90 put the payout ratio at about 83%. That is high for most sectors and typical for tobacco. Last fiscal year, operating cash flow of $6.342 billion minus capex of $551 million left about $5.791 billion in free cash flow. Management is guiding to operating cash flow conversion above 95% and adjusted net debt to EBITDA of 2.0 to 2.5x by year-end, while still running a £1.3 billion buyback. The annual dividend of 245.04p per share rose 2.0%, and ADR dividend records run back to 1999.
Yield: The annualized forward dividend of $3.339404 per ADR on a $60.28 price works out to about 5.5%, which makes this a high-yield name.

Bull case: Smokeless products are driving the growth. BAT reached 34.1 million smokeless consumers after adding 4.7 million, Velo modern oral revenue grew 48% at constant currency, and US Velo Plus revenue rose 310%.

sum: Shares in Diageo (LON: DGE) have staged a notable recovery after a punishing sell-off earlier this year drove the FTSE 100 drinks giant to its lowest levels in years, with technical indicators now flashing renewed bullish momentum.

The stock plunged sharply in late February, tumbling from around 1,874p to below 1,640p in a single session — a drop of more than 12% — as investors reacted to a disappointing trading update highlighting soft demand across key spirits categories, including tequila and premium whisky.

Selling pressure persisted through March, dragging shares to an intraday low near 1,350p, their weakest level in several years, with the Relative Strength Index (RSI) sinking into deeply oversold territory below 27 — a classic signal that the stock had been sold down too far, too fast.

From that base, Diageo began a steady grind higher through the spring and summer. The rally accelerated dramatically in early August, when the shares gapped up from around 1,655p to nearly 1,790p within two sessions — an 8% surge reportedly linked to bullish broker commentary, including from Jefferies, alongside renewed optimism over cost-cutting and portfolio actions.

That move propelled the stock decisively above its 200-day moving average (around 1,558p), a widely watched technical threshold that often signals a shift from a downtrend to a more constructive footing.

sum: Diageo and Pernod Ricard shares are trading near multi-year lows as investors reassess alcohol demand, consumer habits and the outlook for defensive stocks.

The alcohol sector is facing one of its most difficult periods in years. Shares in companies such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard are trading at levels not seen for many years, prompting investors to ask whether the industry is dealing with a lasting slowdown or a temporary sell-off. For investors watching equity markets, and for traders using CFDs, consumer staples are once again becoming a closely watched area of the market.

For a long time, major drinks companies were viewed as resilient defensive stocks. That perception has weakened. After alcohol consumption surged during the pandemic, demand in the US has since fallen by about 7% compared with 2019 levels. Some analysts are now asking whether the alcohol industry could face a challenge similar to the one that reshaped tobacco stocks in previous decades.

The pressure reflects several overlapping trends. Higher living costs have made consumers more selective, younger drinkers appear less attached to traditional alcohol brands, and health-focused behaviour has become more visible. Weight-loss drugs have also added a new uncertainty for the sector, as investors debate whether changing appetite and consumption patterns could affect demand for beer, wine and spirits.

Those risks matter because drinks companies have historically relied on pricing power, brand loyalty and relatively stable demand. If volumes remain under pressure for longer, investors may become less willing to pay premium valuations for businesses that were once treated as defensive compounders.

The counterargument is that valuations already reflect a great deal of bad news. Diageo and Pernod Ricard still own globally recognised brands, have broad distribution networks and remain exposed to long-term demand in emerging markets. If consumers stabilise and margins recover, today’s depressed share prices could begin to look more attractive.
That makes the sector difficult to judge. Low valuations alone do not guarantee a recovery, especially if weaker demand proves structural rather than cyclical.

sum: Investors in Diageo rushed for the exit as the scale of the challenge facing Dave Lewis was laid bare following the new CEO’s maiden set of results.
Lewis, who has been in the job for less than two months, threw the kitchen sink at the spirits giant in a bid to pave the way for a mammoth turnaround mission.
But shareholders reacted in horror as the Guinness maker cut the dividend, slashed its financial outlook and missed growth expectations.

Lewis, who will lay out his full action plan later in the year, also signalled his intention to lower prices to make Diageo more competitive. The City worried about the potential for a price war and a subsequent hit to margins.

Lewis’ first public remarks came after Diageo posted a 2.8% drop in organic sales in the six months to 31 October, which was worse than analysts feared. The company also downgraded profit and sales expectations for 2026 on the back of struggles in the US and China.

And the annual dividend was set at a minimum of 50 cents for FY26 and beyond, compared with 103.5 cents in the previous year. Trevor Stirling of Bernstein expected the move to free up £1bn of cashflow.

Overall, shares recorded their biggest one-day fall in the aftermath on Wednesday, tumbling by as much as 13%. The stock continued its decline today, heading back towards the all-time lows of 1,589p seen at the end of 2025. It means more than £12bn has been wiped off the value of the group in the past year as the share price sank by a quarter following profit warnings and an exit for former boss Debra Crew.

sum: LONDON — European stocks ended higher on Wednesday as global market nerves eased after U.S. President Donald Trump's universal 10% tariff came into effect rather than the threatened higher 15% rate.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed 0.7% higher with most major bourses finishing the day in positive territory.

British spirits company Diageo finished the session down 12.7% after lowering its 2026 sales and profit outlook on Wednesday. The world's biggest spirits maker reported that weaker demand from North America and China had affected earnings in its fiscal first half.

Net sales declined by 4% to $10.5 billion in the six months to December, as the company cited "pressure on disposable income impacting US Spirits." Operating profit was also 1.2% lower at $3.1 billion.

Diageo is now expecting further weakness in 2026, with organic sales projected to be 2% to 3% lower, organic operating profit to be flat to up low single digits, and cut dividends to 20 cents per share.
Additionally, British carmaker Aston Martin will slash 20% of its workforce in 2026 after reporting weaker earnings due to the impact of tariffs in the U.S. and China, it said Wednesday.

Diageo (HY Results): weak first half, guidance lowered
sum: Diageo reported first-half net sales of $10.5bn, down 2.8% on an organic basis, with volumes and average selling prices both falling. This was driven by declines in North America and Asia Pacific, which more than offset growth in other regions.
Underlying operating profit also fell by 2.8% to $3.3bn, with lower marketing investment helping to offset the impact of higher tariff costs.
Free cash flow fell by $0.2bn to $1.5bn. Net debt remained broadly flat at $21.7bn.

Full-year guidance has been lowered again, with organic net sales now expected to decline by 2-3% (previously: flat to slightly down). Organic operating profit growth is now expected to be flat to low-single digits (previously: mid-single digits).
The interim dividend has been cut to 20 cents per share, down 51%.

Diageo’s first-half performance remains weighed down by weakness in the US and China, which led to profit guidance being lowered for the second time this year. Alongside the dividend being cut in half, the shares understandably moved lower on the day.

Diageo is a giant in the alcohol world, with 13 billion-dollar brands on its shelves. Its world-class stable of spirit brands includes the likes of Smirnoff, Johnnie Walker and Tanqueray. In beer, Guinness remains a stout performer, recording yet another period of strong revenue growth.

items.t: Diageo shares rise following report that new CEO plans sweeping executive overhaul
sum: Diageo PLC (LSE:DGE) shares rose 1.8% to 1,813 pence after the Financial Times reported that Dave Lewis, the drinks group's recently appointed chief executive, is planning a significant restructuring of the company's leadership team.

Lewis intends to replace several members of Diageo's 14-person executive committee and remove entire layers of management, the newspaper said, citing people familiar with the matter. Diageo declined to comment.

The reported shake-up comes three months after Diageo, the maker of Johnnie Walker whisky and Guinness, appointed Lewis to lead a turnaround at the world's largest spirits company following a prolonged period of weak performance.

Lewis, a former chief executive of supermarket group Tesco who earned the nickname "Drastic Dave" for his cost-cutting approach, faces considerable challenges at Diageo, including the impact of US tariff increases on the company's most important market.

The group has struggled with sluggish consumer demand across key regions in recent years, prompting the board to look outside the company for leadership capable of delivering a rapid operational overhaul.

Where could the Scottish Mortgage share price finish 2026?
sum: The Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust (LSE:SMT) share price has delivered strong returns for shareholders over the past 12 months. And there are several reasons for this.
An investment trust‘s market value (share price) is driven by supply and demand, influenced by the value of its underlying holdings. This is measured by the Net Asset Value (NAV).
For trusts holding public stocks, the NAV can be updated daily, and it serves as the benchmark to determine if the trust is trading at a discount or a premium.
However, Scottish Mortgage has investments in privately-held companies as well listed stocks, and this does make the NAV a little more challenging.

For some time, the trust’s traded below that NAV figure. One reason is that many investors had their fingers burned in 2021 when growth stocks — which most Scottish Mortgage investments are — plummeted.

Another might simply be the fact that UK-listed companies and trusts don’t typically trade at fair value. That’s been the case for a while, although there’s probably a good case to say that a few banks and other household-name stocks have pushed too high in the recent rally.

Scottish Mortgage has a relatively diverse set of holdings. However, some companies and sectors are more represented than others. When it comes to technology, its hardware investments such as Nvidia and TSMC have vastly outperformed its software holdings including Spotify.

items.t: Is it madness to bet against the Rolls-Royce share price?
sum: Betting against the Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR) share price probably counts as one of the worst strategies on the FTSE 100. We’re talking about a stock that’s rocketed 1,250% in five years and still doesn’t seem to know how to stop.

Investors who banked profits a year ago will be kicking themselves today, with the shares more than doubling in the past 12 months alone. But that’s history. As ever, what matters is what happens next. Can it really keep climbing like this?

Rolls-Royce should have run out of steam months ago. The so-called ‘new manager bounce’ triggered by the appointment of Tufan Erginbilgic began more than three years ago on 1 January 2023. It’s remarkable that he’s still having such an impact.

Erginbilgic famously kicked off his tenure by decrying Rolls-Royce as a “burning platform” and duly administered some shock therapy. Normally, that early impact fades. But it hasn’t, largely because he keeps setting ambitious targets and then beating them with ease.
In full-year 2024, Rolls-Royce reported a 57% jump in underlying operating profit to £2.46bn, while free cash flow surged 88% to £2.43bn. Investors shared in the success, with a £1bn share buyback.
Full-year 2025 results are due on 26 February and guidance remains upbeat. The company is targeting underlying operating profit of £3.1bn to £3.2bn, with free cash flow between £3bn and £3.1bn.

That is, technically, a slowdown. Even at the top end, profit growth would be ‘only’ 26% and cash flow growth 28%. I doubt investors will complain, but there will be plenty of noise if Rolls-Royce undershoots.

items.t: Up 35% in 2026, Europe’s most valuable company is boosting my Stocks and Shares ISA
sum: There are a few stocks in my Stocks and Shares ISA that are doing really well this year. One is ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) – Europe’s most valuable company – which is up about 35%.
How has this stock managed to generate such huge gains so early in the year? Let’s take a look at what’s going on here.

ASML specialises in the design and manufacture of Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems – sophisticated machines that are crucial for the production of advanced computer chips. It’s pretty much the only company in the world that makes these EUV systems so it’s a key player in the current tech/AI revolution. Without its products the tech boom would grind to a halt.

Now this year, companies that play an important role in chip manufacturing have seen their share prices surge. One reason for this is that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co – the world’s largest chip manufacturer – has announced a massive capex increase for 2026.
It plans to spend $52bn-$56bn this year building new manufacturing plants. So it’s essentially going to be writing massive cheques to companies like ASML for equipment.

Another reason for the share price surge this year is that, with all the geopolitical carnage, there’s been more focus on ‘silicon sovereignty’. This is where nations are aiming to control their own semiconductor supply chains to ensure national and economic security.

For the last few decades, the chip industry’s been structured for the lowest possible cost, with a lot of manufacturing taking place in Taiwan and Korea. Now however, governments are optimising for geopolitical safety.

Could £5,000 invested in Rolls-Royce shares now be worth £10,000 by the end of 2026?
sum: Over the past year, the share price of Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR) has more than doubled. Rolls-Royce shares have moved up by an impressive 117% during those 12 months.
Might the same happen in coming months? Could the Rolls-Royce share price double by the end of 2025?
At first mention, that notion might seem fanciful. After all, this is a long-established company in a mature industry.

Over the decades the industry has proven to be cyclical and Rolls’ profit and loss account has moved around substantially. Sudden unexpected drops in civil aviation demand have hammered the share before. I see that as an ongoing risk.

However, the past year has shown that Rolls-Royce shares have a lot of oomph. In fact that is a continuation of a trend that meant the share was among the best FTSE 100 performers of 2023 and 2024, as well as 2025.
That is an impressive track record, but of course in the stock market past performance is not necessarily an indication of what to expect in future.

The meteoric rise of Rolls-Royce shares – up 1,072% in five years – is also partly down to a low base. The pandemic era brought the company to its knees and the shares were selling for pennies as recently as 2022.

items.t: The JD Sports share price has tanked after a broker downgrade. But I remain optimistic
sum: By lunchtime today (6 January), the JD Sports Fashion (LSE:JD.) share price was nearly 7% lower after the Bank of America downgraded the stock. In November, Shore Capital was also downbeat about the retailer’s shares. It said the group’s third quarter (the 13 weeks to 1 November 2025) trading update “underscored the depth of the current trading headwinds“.

Admittedly, the retailer’s latest press release wasn’t very positive. The group said pre-tax profits would be at the lower end of the consensus of estimates (£853m-£888m). And, worryingly, compared to a year earlier, like-for-like (LFL) sales were down 1.7%, with Asia-Pacific being the only region to grow.
Shore Capital was concerned that the group was unable to pass on rising labour and operating costs to customers due to a falling top line.
However, despite this apparent doom and gloom, I remain optimistic about the prospects for JD Sports. Here’s why.
At the moment, I reckon the group’s shares are attractively priced. In fact, they look to be in bargain territory.

Analysts are expecting adjusted basic earnings per share of 11.4p for its current financial year ending in February 2026 (FY26). This means the stock trades on just 7.3 times expected earnings. Looking ahead to FY28, the multiple drops to 6.1. This is incredibly cheap for any business, especially one that’s on the FTSE 100.

And with relatively little borrowing on its balance sheet – it reported net debt (excluding leases) of £125m at 2 August 2025 — it remains impressively cash generative. This is important because it gives it the headroom to spend more on either revamping existing stores or buying additional ones. Alternatively, it could return further cash to shareholders.

Diageo (Announcement): CEO appointed
sum: Incoming CEO, Sir Dave Lewis, is currently on the boards of Haleon and PepsiCo, and was CEO of Tesco from 2014-2020 after three decades at Unilever.
Interim CEO Nik Jhangiani will resume his role as Chief Financial Officer.

Diageo unveiled its new leader in the form of Sir Dave Lewis, which buoyed markets on the day. He’s a big name in the consumer-oriented space. Despite having never worked in spirits before, expectations are high that his strong brands and marketing background can help turn Diageo’s fortunes around.

We’re cautiously optimistic that Sir Dave Lewis has the right toolkit for the job. But as an external hire, it will take him some time to fully grasp the task at hand and form a strategy to address Diageo’s challenges. In the meantime, trading in many of the group’s main markets remains tough.

Diageo is a giant in the alcohol world, with 13 billion-dollar brands on its shelves. Its world-class stable of spirit brands includes the likes of Smirnoff, Johnnie Walker and Tanqueray. In beer, Guinness remains a stout performer, recording yet another period of strong revenue growth.

The past few years have seen a trend towards more premium brands, which has helped to prop up margins in the past. That trend appears to be slowing in most regions, and alongside a soft underlying market, the outlook for sales growth looks muted in the near term.

Tariffs are another issue, and look set to add around $200mn of extra costs annually, or around 3.5% of last year’s underlying operating profits. To help offset this, Diageo’s looking to streamline operations elsewhere in the business, hoping to find a total of $625mn of cost savings over the next three years. Half of this will fall to the bottom line to improve profitability, while the other half’s set to be invested back into the business to drive future growth.

sum: LONDON — European stocks closed lower on Thursday, as investors reacted to another flurry of corporate earnings.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 fell 0.7%, with most sectors and major bourses ending the session in negative territory.
It was a busy day for earnings with quarterly reports from a slew of regional companies.

AstraZeneca held its guidance steady on Thursday morning, after reporting better-than-expected third-quarter revenues and profit. Total revenue, which jumped 10% year-on-year in the third quarter on a constant currency basis, is expected to rise by a high single-digit percentage this year, while core earnings per share are forecast to jump by a low double-digit percentage.
Shares fluctuated above and below the flat line throughout the day, before finishing up 3.1%.

Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday morning, AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said the company had decided to keep its guidance unchanged as it was still grappling with headwinds in China and Latin America.
"We have a range in our guidance; we could end up in the top end of the range. We decided to be cautious and potentially overdeliver if everything goes well," he said.
